Europe's night trains are back, and booking them is still a mess

Published 2026-10-06 23:30 UTC

Night trains have made a real comeback in Europe. Rail operators added about a dozen sleeper routes this year, linking cities such as Brussels and Prague, Paris and Berlin, and Amsterdam and Vienna. Many of the new services sell out on weekends, and operators say demand is strongest among travelers who want to avoid short flights.

Booking those trips is another matter. Each operator runs its own ticketing system, and journeys that cross two or three countries often require separate tickets from separate websites. A passenger who misses a connection because the first train ran late may have no right to rebooking on the second, because the two tickets are legally unrelated contracts.

Ars tried to book a sleeper from Amsterdam to Vienna with a connection onward to Budapest. The night train portion could be booked on the operator's own site, but the daytime connection had to be bought from a different railway, and the combined price was nearly double what a single through ticket would have cost if one existed.

Industry groups blame the absence of common booking standards. European rail companies have discussed shared distribution rules for years, but national operators are reluctant to let third-party sellers access their inventory on equal terms. The European Commission has proposed a regulation that would require through-ticketing and passenger protection across operators, though rail companies are lobbying to soften it.

Sleeper operators also face practical limits. Rolling stock is scarce, and many routes rely on refurbished carriages that are decades old. New sleeper cars on order from manufacturers will not arrive until 2028 at the earliest. Track access fees, which vary widely by country, can make a single overnight run unprofitable even when it is full.

For now, the best advice from frequent rail travelers is to book early, buy the longest single ticket available, and leave generous buffers between connections. Several independent ticketing sites help by searching across operators, but they cannot fix the underlying lack of through-ticket protection.
